title: Rehearsing by head: Buddy and Zeb, George Boyd, Eddie Marsh
summary: Punch says bands rarely rehearsed, praises the Petit-Zeb pairing and names his clarinetist George Boyd and Eddie Marsh.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Well, I was going to ask you about the other fellas. When you got here in the city, did any of them practice long hours or anything?
No. I was practicing a little bit with Jack Kerr, but not very much. Not much.
The bands didn't rehearse much?
No, no. They played by a head, you know. They just called something and go playing it.
Still, they had to work some things out. I guess they'd tell.

Well, yeah. That's why I say a few of the things like, he know the song and I learned it and something in there he wanted me to catch. Well, he tell me, you know. How I'd go and everything, I learned on the horns. Play it in there.
But like now, Buddy, he must have worked things out with Zeb pretty close.
Well, Buddy and Zeb used to be right together all the time. They could sit down and get the stuff together. It was right together.
And Zeb knew when to take the lead and stuff like that, huh?
Mm-hmm.
Zeb knew when to take the lead and stuff like that.
And I see my client-in-player, he used to drive a truck, see. We couldn't have a rehearsal because he'd be on the truck all the time.
Who was that?
George Boyd.
Mm-hmm.
That was my regular client-in-player.
What about Eddie Marsh? Did he work then?
Yeah, he was in the band with me all the way.
He was working?
Yeah, he worked too. Yeah, he used to work.
And you?
No, I wasn't doing nothing. I didn't do nothing.
